trace.goal: Teach one concrete operator lesson with specific examples and conviction.
expected_facts: The answer should define the NRR problem clearly: a company with weak expansion or unhealthy retention despite still appearing alive.
It should recommend concrete responses such as fixing product value, segmentation, onboarding, pricing, or customer success.
It should stress that weak NRR becomes a structural drag on growth.
rubric_must_haves: Defines the term in plain language.
Explains why the condition is dangerous.
Offers specific operational fixes rather than abstract encouragement.
Sounds direct and urgent without being melodramatic.
trace.gold_reference: A strong answer should explain that an 'NRR zombie' is a company that can still grow on the surface but lacks the expansion and retention engine needed for healthy compounding. The founder takeaway is to diagnose the root cause quickly and fix the product, segmentation, pricing, or customer outcomes before the weakness hardens into a permanent ceiling.

trace.answer:
Q:  I’m an SaaS founder who’s seen his NRR go from ~130% to <80%. My customers complain constantly, have asked me to turn off auto-payments, etc. How do I get out of this hole? The best thing you can do is raise prices on existing customers by 10%-15%.
At first, folks will complain. But then they’ll stop complaining. And your revenue will grow — at least somewhat — without adding any new customers. In fact, with most B2B products, pricing almost always increases net retention.
That won’t save you per se, but it can buy you some time.
Second, invest in your top logos and accounts. They’re all you really have left. Try to push them upmarket, try to drive their usage up. That will also help improve NRR a bit.
Third, understand you have just one shot to change things. You need to increase renewal rates dramatically to climb out of this hole. Forcing everyone to log back into portal every quarter isn’t going to work. Neither is making small changes. It’s too little, too late. You can only jump out of the NRR zombie hole once.
And finally, make sure your existing customers love you. Make them happy. That’s how we win, and why we keep our customers, forever. Not because they don’t churn — they all do eventually. But because they stay longer, spend more, and recommend us.
Go talk to the top 50 customers yourself now. Right now. This week. Call them, email them, visit them in-person. Ask them what you could do better. Ask them why they didn’t ask for price increases themselves. Ask them if they’d be willing to pay a premium today.
Listen carefully, and take action based on what they say. You can fix a lot in Q1. Maybe enough to move the needle on NRR. But you probably aren’t going to see improvement before the end of the year. So start now.
NRR Zombies (SaaStr Annual Video)
Here’s the deal. A while back, there was a video from the SaaStr Annual that sort of got lost over time, but came up recently again. “What happens when you let NRR slip below 100?”
I think the answer is pretty clear:
It starts to spiral down. From 115% to 110% to 105% to 95%. Because no one wants to pay more than $X a month for something mediocre.

retrieval_hits.text:
1. NRR is destiny.
When NRR drops below 110%, alarm bells should go off. Below 100%, you’re in serious trouble. Monitor this metric religiously.

#4.  Don’t settle for less growth than Your NRR + 20%
.
E.g., if your NRR is 120%, even if times are tougher, don’t settle for growing at least +40% next year. Don’t hide in excuses and a high NRR.  Don’t hide in renewals and in your CRO forcing the base to pay more.  Force yourself to at least grow +20% more than your NRR.

#4.  Don’t settle for less growth than Your NRR + 20%
.  E.g., if your NRR is 120%, even if times are tougher, don’t settle for growing at least +40% next year.  Not all your customer base has evaporated.  Don’t hide in excuses and a high NRR.  Don’t hide in renewals.  Don’t force your base to pay more than they want to.  Force yourself to at least grow +20% more than your NRR.

2. NRR is the canary in the coal mine.
Snowflake’s decline from 158% to 125% foreshadowed everything else. If your best customers aren’t expanding, you have a problem.
